run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_223 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary:
Two user tables exist in the configured SQL Server database (target m0-otel-20260909, database read at query time 2026-11-22T10:11:48Z–10:12:33Z, after the authorized window ending 2026-11-22T10:11:46Z): dbo.holmes_eval_223 and dbo.orders. The verification code stored in dbo.holmes_eval_223 (row id=1, category eval_test) is HOLMES-MSSQL-EVAL-223-j2w7p9.

Slow-query analysis: dbo.orders (10,000 rows, 64 pages) has exactly one index, the clustered primary key PK__orders__3213E83FA20696AF on id; there is no index with customer_id as a key column. Because customer_id is not a leading key of any index, WHERE customer_id = <value> cannot seek and must scan the whole clustered index: index usage stats show user_seeks = 0 and user_scans = 5 on that clustered index, and an equivalent predicate query (customer_id = 12345) was observed in the plan cache with 64 logical reads for one execution — exactly the 64 used pages of the table, i.e. a full scan. SQL Server's own missing-index DMV independently recommends an index with equality_columns = [customer_id] for dbo.orders (avg_user_impact 93.98, user_seeks 1). Statistics are not the problem: an auto-created statistics object on customer_id exists with 10,000 of 10,000 rows sampled. Blocking is not supported as the cause: at query time only this session's own statement was running, with no wait type observed.

Two secondary observations: (a) SELECT * forces all five columns (id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status) to be returned, so a non-covering index still needs key lookups; (b) the literal 12345 is outside the data actually stored — customer_id ranges 1..1000 with 1,000 distinct values over 10,000 rows, and customer_id = 12345 currently matches 0 rows — yet even that predicate must scan the table. The user's exact statement text 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345' was not present in the plan cache, so its own measured elapsed time is unknown; the scan conclusion rests on the index layout, the index usage counters, the missing-index DMV and the 64 logical reads of an equivalent predicate query.

Index usage statistics for the dbo.orders clustered index show user_seeks = 0, user_scans = 5, user_lookups = 0 and user_updates = 10000, i.e. every observed read of this table was a scan, never a seek.

SQL Server's missing-index DMV reports for table orders an equality-column recommendation on [customer_id] (no inequality or included columns), with user_seeks = 1, avg_total_user_cost 0.0643 and avg_user_impact 93.98.

A predicate query on customer_id = 12345 in the plan cache (execution_count 1, total_elapsed_time 783 microseconds, total_logical_reads 64) read 64 pages, which equals the 64 used pages of the dbo.orders clustered index — consistent with a full clustered index scan rather than a targeted seek.
customer_id in dbo.orders spans 1 to 1000 with 1,000 distinct values across 10,000 rows (about 10 rows per customer), and the literal 12345 matches 0 rows in the current data.

An auto-created statistics object on dbo.orders.customer_id (_WA_Sys_00000002_38996AB5) exists with rows = 10000 and rows_sampled = 10000, last_updated 2026-11-22T10:11:57.533 (the time of this investigation's own predicate query), so cardinality statistics for customer_id are present and fully sampled.

At query time the only user session visible in sys.dm_exec_requests was this investigation's own statement in 'running' state with no wait type and no blocking reported, so no concurrent blocking or lock wait was observed to explain slow performance.

Blocking or lock contention on dbo.orders as the cause of the slow query was considered and rejected: no blocking session or wait type was visible for the only running statement at query time, whereas the index layout and scan counters explain the full-table read directly.

The primary supported reason SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 is slow is the absence of a nonclustered index keyed on customer_id in dbo.orders: with only the clustered primary key on id, the optimizer has no seek path on customer_id and must scan all 64 pages (and would scale linearly as rows grow), with an additional per-row key-lookup cost if a non-covering index existed because SELECT * projects all five columns.

Advice: create a nonclustered index on dbo.orders keyed on customer_id and INCLUDE the remaining projected columns (order_date, total_amount, status) so the predicate can seek and the query becomes covered, e.g. CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_orders_customer_id ON dbo.orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (order_date, total_amount, status); this matches the DMV's equality-column recommendation on [customer_id].

Advice: replace SELECT * with an explicit column list (for example id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status), which keeps the covering index smaller and avoids reading columns the caller does not use; and validate the literal 12345, because customer_id currently ranges only 1..1000, so the tested value matches no rows even though a scan is still performed.
